The share of the extreme poor living in a fragile and conflict-affected situation (FCS) rose from 12 percent in 2010 to 57 percent in 2026, as more high-poverty economies became fragile and because extreme poverty fell more quickly in non-FCS economies. By 2030, 87 percent of the extreme poor globally will be living in Sub-Saharan Africa or in an FCS economy or both. • If the per capita economic growth rates observed over 2015–24 persist, the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will increase by 2030: an unprecedented reversal of the decades-long decline. Population growth in high-poverty economies is a key factor in the potential increase.

results.text: Sub-Saharan Africa, in contrast, experienced much more modest improvement.2 There, extreme poverty rates declined from 62 percent in 1990 to 43 percent in 2026. The extreme poverty rate has declined little in the region since 2014. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region (refer to box 1.4 for information on World Bank regional classifications), extreme poverty has been increasing in recent years. In both regions, low rates of per capita economic growth have undermined efforts to reduce poverty (Beegle et al. 2016).

results.text: After decades of progress, the reduction in extreme poverty has ground to a halt After decades of significant and steady progress, the reduction of global poverty has reached a critical juncture. In 1990, nearly 2.3 billion people—43 percent of the global population—were living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $3.00-a-person-a-day (in 2021 PPP terms) (refer to box 1.1). By 2019, the number had fallen dramatically, to 837 million people, or 10.8 percent of the global population. But, since then, virtually no progress on reducing extreme poverty has been made. The COVID-19 pandemic triggered the largest setback in decades (Mahler et al. 2022). In 2026, 811 million people—1 in 10 globally—were living in extreme poverty, and this rate has remained essentially unchanged since 2020. results.text: To investigate the disproportionate impact, two methods allow variation in the intensity of the shock faced by households (Kimura et al. 2026). In both cases, the average growth of the economy is maintained at the level indicated in Global Economic Prospects, June 2026 (World Bank 2026c), which captures the aggregate income and price shock. First, households are allocated sectoral growth rates based on their sector of employment. Second, inflation is allocated to households depending on their budget’s exposure to food and energy. Poorer households typically spend a greater share on food and energy and thus receive lower real income if the prices of these items rise. A distribution-neutral assumption, which is used as the baseline throughout the report, would instead assume the equal distribution of inflationary shocks.

results.text: Applying the vulnerability approach to the World Bank’s harmonized household surveys—estimating, for each economy, the probability that a household is living on less than the poverty line of the relevant income group over a few years, and identifying the consumption level at which this probability becomes low—yields economic security lines of about $6.00, $7.00, and $14.00 a day for the three income groups. This is roughly twice the corresponding poverty lines, but with wide variation across economies (Bolch et al. 2026). The threshold also shifts with the risks households face. In Europe and Central Asia, the income needed to maintain a low probability of falling into poverty rose by about 10 percent in real terms between 2008 and 2018 as the shocks pushing households into poverty grew larger (Bussolo et al. 2025). results.text: 25 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration BOX 1.4 The Poverty and Inequality Platform has been updated with new data and revised regional classifications The data on poverty and inequality used throughout the report are available through the World Bank’s online tool for statistics on poverty, inequality, and shared prosperity: the Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP). The PIP data build primarily on national household surveys and are usually updated twice a year as national statistical offices around the world make new data available. The availability of recent survey data is crucial for the accuracy and reliability of the platform’s estimates of poverty and shared prosperity.
